note: A faithful rendering of the commentary's glosses on the Prajñāpāramitā passage; a few loose phrasings ('apprehended' for being embraced by roots of virtue, transitive 'cease'), but nothing that changes the argument.

Sound rendering of the list of bodhisattva qualities (respect for the teacher, pure livelihood, forest dwelling, the bhūmis); only the opening fragment, cut off at the side boundary from the face-lotus simile, reads awkwardly.

errors.english: He cut his hair along with its various head-ornaments as if harvesting the blue petals of a lotus.
errors.why: 'Blue as an utpala petal' describes the sword he draws (Buddhacarita 6.57 utpalapattranīla); he then cuts off his crown together with his hair, so there is no simile of harvesting petals.

fix.find: Then, emerging like a serpent from its hole, he drew out the sword. He cut his hair along with its various head-ornaments as if harvesting the blue petals of a lotus.
fix.replace: Then he drew out the sword, blue as the petal of a blue lotus, like a serpent from its hole, and cut off his variegated crown together with his hair.

errors.english: the assembly of gods and the most exalted among the deities performed the worship
errors.why: The hosts of gods honoured the hair with excellent divine offerings; 'ལྷ་ཡི་ཁྱད་པར་འཕགས་པ་' is the means of worship, not a second group of worshippers.

errors.english: he saw a hunter wearing a garment marked with the color of a golden swan in the forest. Being steadfast, he felt a desire for those clothes.
errors.why: No hunter is in this verse: seeing his own garment marked with golden geese, the steadfast one longed for a forest garment; the hunter appears only in the next verse.

fix.find: he saw a hunter wearing a garment marked with the color of a golden swan in the forest. Being steadfast, he felt a desire for those clothes.
fix.replace: seeing his own garment marked with golden swans, the steadfast one longed for a garment of the forest.

errors.english: possessing the body of a blue deer
errors.why: The deity takes the form of a deer-hunter (Skt. mṛgavyādha; སྔོན་པོ is very likely a corruption of རྔོན་པ), as the hunter's speech that follows confirms.

errors.english: The King of the Shakyas
errors.why: སྐྱེས = born of: the speaker is the son of the Śākya king (śākyarājaprabhava), not the king.

errors.english: if you have no attachment to peace in this place
errors.why: ཞི་བ is a vocative ('gentle one', Skt. saumya) and འདིར refers to the robe: 'so, gentle sir, if you are not attached to this'.

fix.find: if you have no attachment to peace in this place
fix.replace: gentle sir, if you are not attached to this robe

errors.english: Please take it and wear these white ones.
errors.why: The hunter asks to be given the white garment in exchange (Skt. prati yaccha śuklam); he then takes the white garment himself.

fix.find: Please take it and wear these white ones.
fix.replace: Please take it, and give me that white one in return.

errors.english: Having turned back his followers whose faces were wet with tears
errors.why: འདུན་པ is the proper name Chandaka (the groom), whom he sends back with tear-stained face, not a group of followers.

fix.find: Having turned back his followers whose faces were wet with tears
fix.replace: Having sent back Chandaka, whose face was wet with tears

note: The Great Departure episode in Buddhacarita 6: the overall sequence is right, but several verses are misconstrued (the sword simile, the garment, the hunter's request, Chandaka read as 'followers').

errors.english: between the breasts of the Bhagavan Blessed Lord and the Goddesses
errors.why: It means the Bhagavān and the one named consort-goddess; the four goddesses are treated separately below, so the plural 'Goddesses' blurs the two steps.

errors.english: the highly praised white, red, and black syllables (Om), (Ah), and (Hum)
errors.why: རབ་བསྔགས = praṇava, i.e. the syllable OṂ itself, not an epithet 'highly praised' (the same calque recurs in 'the highly praised syllables and so forth')

fix.find: One should visualize the highly praised white, red, and black syllables
fix.replace: One should visualize the white, red, and black syllables

errors.english: the water of faith
errors.why: ཡེ་ཤེས་ཀྱི་ཆུ = water of gnosis (jñāna), the standard empowerment-flask water.

note: The sādhana sequence (blessing of body, speech and mind, summoning and merging the jñāna-maṇḍala, empowerment) is followed correctly, but there are two ritual-term errors and a typo in the dharmadhātu mantra.

errors.english: even if the objective reality is not as described
errors.why: Continuing དོན་གྱི་དེ་ཉིད་ཡོད་ from the previous side: even if the matter really is so, his speech is false (because he has altered his perception), so it is a saṅghāvaśeṣa.

fix.find: even if the objective reality is not as described
fix.replace: even if the matter is in fact real

errors.english: This is not because both truth and falsehood are connected to perception, rather than being connected to the objective reality of the matter.
errors.why: The Tibetan gives this as the reason: falsehood and truth depend on perception, not on objective fact.

fix.find: This is not because both truth and falsehood are connected to perception, rather than being connected to the objective reality of the matter.
fix.replace: This is because truth and falsehood are connected to perception, not to the objective reality of the matter.

errors.english: when making a false accusation of a fundamental downfall against one who is pure
errors.why: མ་དག་པ = impure: the two sūtra passages ground the offense of accusing even a monk who is in fact fallen, which is the point of the argument.

fix.find: when making a false accusation of a fundamental downfall against one who is pure
fix.replace: when accusing of a fundamental downfall even one who is impure (actually fallen)

errors.english: when the words used to make an accusation of a (Sanghadisesa) are unclear in meaning
errors.why: The accusation is of a pārājika made unclearly; it is the words themselves that bring about (constitute) the saṅghāvaśeṣa.

errors.english: who has committed a (Parajika) offense of defeat through excessive conduct
errors.why: ལྷག་པར་སྤྱོད་པ (adhyācāra) means committing or transgressing a pārājika, not 'excessive conduct'; the same calque recurs below.

note: The Vinaya argument on baseless accusation is inverted in three places (fact versus perception, the negated reason, pure versus impure), so the legal reasoning reads backwards; the anyabhāgīya section is closer to the Tibetan.

errors.english: One is desired to be liberated.
errors.why: འདོད here means 'is held to be': because the mind is released, the eighth is regarded as a liberation (vimokṣa).

fix.find: One is desired to be liberated.
fix.replace: Therefore it is held to be a liberation (vimoksha).

errors.english:
the precious wheel, the lotus,
The sword, and the eight pillars
errors.why: The eight liberations, purified, are the eight pillars, marked with wheel, jewel, lotus and sword; they are not four emblems plus the pillars, and the jewel is merged into 'precious wheel'.

errors.english: The remainder is that which performs the evening ritual
errors.why: After the seven suns for the seats, 'night-maker' most likely means the moon: the remaining seats are moon discs, not an evening rite.

note: The verse is kept as verse and the eight vimokṣas are mostly right, but the palace-symbolism mappings are garbled in several places.

errors.english: a contradiction with a treatise that one has accepted as a peer
errors.why: It is a treatise that amounts to (is equivalent to) one's own acceptance, so contradicting it is contradicting one's own words; 'as a peer' is wrong.

errors.english: What is a contradiction with renown?
errors.why: གྲགས་པ here is pratīti/prasiddhi, the logical fault of a thesis contradicted by common recognition (conventional usage), not 'renown'; the calque recurs through the rest of the side.

fix.find: What is a contradiction with renown?
fix.replace: What is a contradiction with common recognition (pratiti)?

note: The thesis-fault discussion (own words, treatise, common recognition) is followed in outline, but the key logical term is mistranslated and the last passage on conventional denotation is muddy.

errors.english: (ayoniso-manasikara) unwise attention
errors.why: This is a Sanskrit Abhidharmakośa commentary, so the equivalent is ayoniśomanaskāra; the gloss gives the Pali form.

note: A sound rendering of Yaśomitra's discussion of fruits and of 'respectively' (yathākramam), with the Kośa verses correctly identified.

errors.english: Hold the cord level with the center.
errors.why: ལྟེ་བ here most likely means the navel: the cord is held at navel height, which is why the commentary says the maṇḍala is drawn in the air.

note: The commentary on consecrating the site, the cords, and drawing in the air and then on the ground is rendered faithfully, with one doubtful reading of ལྟེ་བ.

errors.english: its simultaneous existence with physical objects
errors.why: This finishes འཇུག་པའི་རྣམ་པར་ཤེས་པ་དང་ལྷན་[ཅིག] from the previous side: simultaneity with the active consciousnesses, not with physical objects.

fix.find: through its simultaneous existence with physical objects
fix.replace: through its simultaneous existence with the active consciousnesses

note: The Viniścayasaṃgrahaṇī passage on the ālaya as root of saṃkleśa (beings' world, vessel world, truths of suffering and origin) is accurate apart from the invented first term.
